Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
DETAILED ACTION
1.		This Office Action is responsive to the communication filed 3/09/2022.
Information Disclosure Statement
2.	The information disclosure statement (IDS) submitted on 3/09/2022 was filed after the mailing date of the instant application. The submission is in compliance with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97. Accordingly, the information disclosure statement is being considered by the examiner.
Allowable Subject Matter
3.	Claims 6, 13-14, 17, and 20 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Claim Rejections – 35 USC 103
4.	The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains.  Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
5.	Claims 1-5, 7-12, 15-16, and 18-19 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Vendelbo et al (US 2018/0352433) in view of Jun et al (US 2015/0278506).
Regarding claim 1, Vendelbo et al teaches an authentication method of a first device to a second device (fig. 1, ‘8/’10), the method comprising at least two successive verification operations (par [0014], “second authentication request”), each operation comprising, successively:
generating, by the second device, a first data from a second data generated in a preceding verification operation (par [0135], which discloses the secondary device generating a challenge value corresponding to the first authentication);
sending, by the second device, the first data to the first device (fig. 2, ‘108 & par [0135], which discloses transmitting the information to the user application of the first device);
outputting, by the second device, information indicating whether the verification was successful (par [0023], “first authentication data is successfully verified”), and the second data used by the following verification operation fig. 2, ‘112 & (par [0006], lines 10-16, “second authentication data”);
authenticating the first device to the second device in response to:
for each verification operation, the information indicating that the verification was successful (par [0006], lines 10-16, “second authentication data is successful”).
Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach generating, by the first device, third data and fourth data used by a following verification operation, by applying a first function taking as input at least the first data and the fourth data generated in the preceding verification operation; sending, by the first device, the third data to the second device; verifying, by the second device, the third data using a second function taking as input the first data and the third data; and the fourth data of the first device and the second data of the second device of the preceding verification operation being correct.
However, Jun et al teaches generating, by the first device, third data and fourth data used by a following verification operation (fig. 4, fig 6, par [0009] & par [0050], lines 10-20, which disclose first user device creating pairing data associated with proof and the first challenge information), by applying a first function taking as input at least the first data and the fourth data generated in the preceding verification operation (fig. 4 & par [0050], lines 12-16, “first function”);
sending, by the first device, the third data to the second device (par [0022], lines 6-8, “transmitted from the primary device to the secondary device”);
verifying, by the second device, the third data using a second function taking as input the first data and the third data (par [0021], lines 1-10 par [0031], lines 1-10, which disclose performing secondary functions for authentication using the pairing data); and
the fourth data of the first device and the second data of the second device of the preceding verification operation being correct (par [0015], lines 9-14 & par [0021], lines 7-20, which disclose using the received pairing data to perform secondary functions to generate another proof based on the previous pairing data used to determine previous authentication status, in order to update the authentication status).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al would provide the predictive result of improving upon determining device authentication by using previous authentication status data (as disclosed in par [0021] of Jun et al) because this technique would lower the amount of time needed by Vendelbo et al to authenticate devices by allowing Vendelbo et al to base authentication of communication devices upon credentials provided by each device in the prior collected authentication status.
Regarding claim 2, Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein, during implementation of a first verification operation, the second device uses fifth data to generate the first data, and the first device uses sixth data to generate the third data and the fourth data.
However, Jun et al teaches wherein, during implementation of a first verification operation, the second device uses fifth data to generate the first data (par [0021], lines 1-10, “generate a proof based on a portion of the pairing data”), and the first device uses sixth data to generate the third data and the fourth data (par [0021], lines 1-10, “generate another proof based on a portion of the pairing data”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 1.
Regarding claim 3, Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein the fifth data is different for each verification operation, and the sixth data is different for each verification operation.
However, Jun et al teaches wherein the fifth data is different for each verification operation (fig. 8, which discloses each generated challenge corresponds to different values), and the sixth data is different for each verification operation (fig. 8).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 1.
Regarding claim 4, Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein, during implementation of each verification operation, the second device uses the fifth data to generate the first data, and the first device uses the sixth data to generate the third data and the fourth data.
However, Jun et al teaches wherein, during implementation of each verification operation, the second device uses the fifth data to generate the first data (par [0044], lines 10-14, which discloses generating the first proof based on the received pairing data), and the first device uses the sixth data to generate the third data and the fourth data (par [0022], lines 1-10 and par [0035], lines 28-30,  which disclose the primary device generating the proof and pairing data using retrieved secondary challenge data).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 1.
Regarding claim 5, Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein the second device generates the first data from the second data generated in the preceding verification operation and the fifth data, and the first function takes as input the first data, the fourth data generated in the preceding verification operation, and the sixth data.
However, Jun et al teaches wherein the second device generates the first data from the second data generated in the preceding verification operation and the fifth data (par [0035], lines 34-36, “generated by the secondary device”), and the first function takes as input the first data, the fourth data generated in the preceding verification operation, and the sixth data (par [0037], lines 14-17, “first cryptographic function may be performed based on inputs of the key and first challenge information”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 1.
Regarding claim 7, Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein the first function of one of the at least two successive verification operations is different from the first function of another one of the at least two successive verification operations.
However, Jun et al teaches wherein the first function of one of the at least two successive verification operations is different from the first function of another one of the at least two successive verification operations (par [0021], lines 1-10, “multiple cryptographic functions”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 1.
Regarding claim 8, Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein the first function of one of the at least two successive verification operations is different from the first function of another one of the at least two successive verification operations.
However, Jun et al teaches wherein the first function of one of the at least two successive verification operations is different from the first function of another one of the at least two successive verification operations (par [0033], lines 1-5, “cryptographic functions 412, 413, and 440”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 1.
Regarding claim 9, Vendelbo et al and Jun et al teach the limitations of claim 1.
Vendelbo et al further teaches wherein the first and second devices send data to each other in an encrypted manner (fig. 2 & par [0108]).
Regarding claim 10, Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein, during implementation of each of the at least two successive verification operations, the first and second devices send the data to each other in the encrypted manner using a first encryption key.
However, Jun et al teaches wherein, during implementation of each of the at least two successive verification operations, the first and second devices send the data to each other in the encrypted manner using a first encryption key (par [0039], lines 8-13, which discloses using a stored key to perform cryptographic communication between the first and secondary devices).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 1.
Regarding claim 11, Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein the first encryption key is different for each implementation of each of the at least two successive verification operations.
However, Jun et al teaches wherein the first encryption key is different for each implementation of each of the at least two successive verification operations (claim 9, “generated random number”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 1.
Regarding claim 12, Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein the first encryption key depends on the first encryption key of the preceding verification operation.
However, Jun et al teaches wherein the first encryption key depends on the first encryption key of the preceding verification operation (fig. 8 & par [0050], lines 1-10).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 1.
Regarding claim 15, Vendelbo et al teaches a first device (fig. 1, ‘8/’10), comprising:
a non-transitory memory (par [0008], lines 1-5) comprising instructions; and
a processor in communication with the non-transitory memory (par [0008], lines 1-5, “processing unit”), wherein the processor executes the instructions to authenticate the first device to a second device, at least two successive verification operations (fig. 1, ‘8/’10 & par [0014], “second authentication”), each operation comprising, successively:
receiving first data from the second device, the first data generated by the second device from a second data generated in a preceding verification operation (par [0135], which discloses the secondary device generating a challenge value corresponding to the first authentication);
receiving, from the second device, information indicating whether the verification was successful (par [0023], “first authentication data is successfully verified”), and the second data used by the following verification operation fig. 2, ‘112 & (par [0006], lines 10-16, “second authentication data”);
authenticating the first device to the second device in response to:
for each verification operation, the information indicating that the verification was successful (par [0006], lines 10-16, “second authentication data is successful”).
Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach generating third data and fourth data used by a following verification operation, by applying a first function taking as input at least the first data and the fourth data generated in the preceding verification operation; sending the third data to the second device for verification using a second function taking as input the first data and the third data; and the fourth data of the first device and the second data of the second device of the preceding verification operation being correct.
However, Jun et al teaches generating third data and fourth data used by a following verification operation (fig. 4, fig 6, par [0009] & par [0050], lines 10-20, which disclose first user device creating pairing data associated with proof and the first challenge information), by applying a first function taking as input at least the first data and the fourth data generated in the preceding verification operation (fig. 4 & par [0050], lines 12-16, “first function”);
sending the third data to the second device (par [0022], lines 6-8, “transmitted from the primary device to the secondary device”) for verification using a second function taking as input the first data and the third data (par [0021], lines 1-10 par [0031], lines 1-10, which disclose performing secondary functions for authentication using the pairing data); and
the fourth data of the first device and the second data of the second device of the preceding verification operation being correct (par [0015], lines 9-14 & par [0021], lines 7-20, which disclose using the received pairing data to perform secondary functions to generate another proof based on the previous pairing data used to determine previous authentication status, in order to update the authentication status).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al would provide the predictive result of improving upon determining device authentication by using previous authentication status data (as disclosed in par [0021] of Jun et al) because this technique would lower the amount of time needed by Vendelbo et al to authenticate devices by allowing Vendelbo et al to base authentication of communication devices upon credentials provided by each device in the prior collected authentication status.
Regarding claim 16, Vendelbo et al and Jun et al teach the limitations of claim 15.
Vendelbo et al further teaches wherein the non-transitory memory is configured to store the first (fig. 2, ‘108) and second data (fig. 2, ‘112), and the information (fig. 2, ‘106).
Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein the non-transitory memory is configured to store the third (par [0021], lines 1-10 par [0031], lines 1-10, “pairing data”), and fourth data (par [0009], “proof associated with pairing data”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 15.
Regarding claim 18, Vendelbo et al teaches a second device (fig. 1, ‘8/’10), comprising:
a non-transitory memory (par [0008], lines 1-5) comprising instructions; and
a processor in communication with the non-transitory memory (par [0008], lines 1-5, “processing unit”), wherein the processor executes the instructions to authenticate the first device to a second device, at least two successive verification operations (fig. 1, ‘8/’10 & par [0014], “second authentication”), each operation comprising, successively:
generating a first data from a second data generated in a preceding verification operation (par [0135], which discloses the secondary device generating a challenge value corresponding to the first authentication);
sending the first data to the first device (fig. 2, ‘108 & par [0135], which discloses transmitting the information to the user application of the first device);
outputting information indicating whether the verification was successful (par [0023], “first authentication data is successfully verified”), and the second data used by the following verification operation fig. 2, ‘112 & (par [0006], lines 10-16, “second authentication data”);
authenticating the first device to the second device in response to:
for each verification operation, the information indicating that the verification was successful (par [0006], lines 10-16, “second authentication data is successful”).
Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach receiving third data from the first device, the third and fourth data, used by a following verification operation, generated by the first device by applying a first function taking as input at least the first data and the fourth data generated in the preceding verification operation; verifying the third data using a second function taking as input the first data and the third data; and the fourth data of the first device and the second data of the second device of the preceding verification operation being correct.
However, Jun et al teaches receiving third data from the first device, the third and fourth data, used by a following verification operation (fig. 4, fig 6, par [0009] & par [0050], lines 10-20, which disclose first user device creating pairing data associated with proof and the first challenge information), generated by the first device by applying a first function taking as input at least the first data and the fourth data generated in the preceding verification operation (fig. 4 & par [0050], lines 12-16, “first function”);
verifying the third data using a second function taking as input the first data and the third data (par [0021], lines 1-10 par [0031], lines 1-10, which disclose performing secondary functions for authentication using the pairing data); and
the fourth data of the first device and the second data of the second device of the preceding verification operation being correct (par [0015], lines 9-14 & par [0021], lines 7-20, which disclose using the received pairing data to perform secondary functions to generate another proof based on the previous pairing data used to determine previous authentication status, in order to update the authentication status).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al would provide the predictive result of improving upon determining device authentication by using previous authentication status data (as disclosed in par [0021] of Jun et al) because this technique would lower the amount of time needed by Vendelbo et al to authenticate devices by allowing Vendelbo et al to base authentication of communication devices upon credentials provided by each device in the prior collected authentication status.
Regarding claim 19, Vendelbo et al and Jun et al teach the limitations of claim 18.
Vendelbo et al further teaches wherein the non-transitory memory is configured to store the first (fig. 2, ‘108) and second data (fig. 2, ‘112), and the information (fig. 2, ‘106).
Vendelbo et al does not explicitly teach wherein the non-transitory memory is configured to store the third (par [0021], lines 1-10 par [0031], lines 1-10, “pairing data”), and fourth data (par [0009], “proof associated with pairing data”).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective date of the claimed invention to combine the disclosure of Jun et al within the teachings of Vendelbo et al, according to the motivation disclosed regarding claim 15.
Conclusion
